entry.title: JWT Explained for Beginners — With Simple Math Analogies
entry.summary:
When a user logs in, the server needs to remember who they are on every request. One way is sessions, but that means storing data on the server. JWT solves this differently — all the user info like user ID, roles, and expiry is packed into the token itself, so the server just verifies the signature on each request without hitting the database every time. A JWT, or JSON Web Token, is made of three parts joined by dots: Header, Payload, and Signature. header.payload.signature The Header tells us which algorithm was used to sign the token — like HS256 or RS256 — along with the token type. The Payload holds the actual user data, called "claims" — things like the user's ID, their role, when the token was issued (iat), and when it expires (exp). Common claims are: sub → Subject (user ID)
